ut_notch_the.blurb: A scatter of big boulders in the desert west of Nephi, sitting on both sides of the highway at roughly 5,500 feet. The bouldering covers the whole range, from easy V0 slabs and short pocketed problems up through hard overhangs and dynos in the V7 to V10 zone, with a handful of top-rope and sport lines mixed in. Ratings for most problems are middling, so treat it as a quiet local spot rather than a destination circuit. Little shade information exists, so plan around the desert sun. Bring pads for the taller blocks.
ut_notch_the.parking_note: Roughly 13 miles west of Nephi on Highway 132, the boulders appear beside the road. Use the gravel pullout on the highway's north side; blocks stand on both sides.

ut_4x4.blurb: A broad buttress of Indian Creek sandstone beside Beef Basin Road, made up of finger-to-hand-sized crack lines on a face that holds many 5.11s alongside some 5.10 and harder testpieces. Dark varnish gives many of the best lines unusually clean rock, though lichen, a few loose flakes and dusty crack interiors are normal because traffic is lighter than at the famous Creek walls. Most popular lines stay shaded, which makes it a fine choice when the sun makes other walls uncomfortable. Bring a standard Creek rack with extra thin hands and finger-sized pieces.
ut_4x4.parking_note: Pull off on Beef Basin Road just beyond the second cattle guard; the buttress is the first one on the right side as you head in.
ut_4x4.approach: A trail angles right, then climbs steeply with a bit of easy scrambling to reach the base of the wall.

ut_sinbad_wall_aka_nuclear_wall.blurb: A small, quiet buttress right in the middle of Indian Creek's busy stretch of road. Nearly all of the climbing is crack trad on Wingate sandstone, mostly 5.10 and 5.11 with a few easier and harder lines, and most pitches are short. It is not as impressive up close as it looks from the car, but it offers several good moderates and sees fewer parties than neighboring walls, so it works well as a low-stress warm-up or an overflow choice. Stay off the sandstone when it is damp, as the rock is fragile then.
ut_sinbad_wall_aka_nuclear_wall.parking_note: Gravel pullouts sit along the road on either side of the buttress, between Battle of the Bulge and Scorpion Corner.

ut_schoolroom_area_2.blurb: The western end of Gate Buttress in Little Cottonwood Canyon, just beyond Green Adjective Gully. The granite is excellent, and the area mixes friendly 5.6 to 5.8 crack lines, which draw plenty of beginners and multi-pitch parties, with harder face climbs and some sport routes up to the low 5.12s. Most routes are trad. Many parties come down by the Schoolroom rappels near the mouth of the gully, so a 60 m rope is handy. The wall takes a lot of sun, so expect heat on summer afternoons and crowds on nice weekends.
ut_schoolroom_area_2.parking_note: About 1.25 miles up Little Cottonwood Canyon, use the lot on the left or the roadside on the right.
ut_schoolroom_area_2.approach: From the lot, head west along the trail to the Gate Boulders, bear left into the talus, and work uphill along the western edge of the trees to the base of the buttress.

ut_kelly_s_rock.blurb: A north-facing limestone wall above a dry wash in the Woodbury Road crags, southwest of St. George. Every route is bolted sport climbing with fixed anchors, and the grades spread evenly from the high 5.6 and 5.7s through the 5.9s, 5.10s and 5.11s into the 5.12s and a few 5.13s, so there is something for most levels. A single 60 m rope covers it. The wall shares a short walk with the neighboring Black and Tan crag. The north aspect helps in warmer weather, and the road is graded dirt that a low car can manage.
ut_kelly_s_rock.parking_note: From the Woodbury Road turnoff, drive the graded dirt road a little under four miles and pull in on the right just beyond the fourth cattle guard. The same lot serves Black and Tan.
ut_kelly_s_rock.approach: Walk back to the wash and follow it up to the right, or take the cairned shortcut across the corner. It is around a fifth of a mile to the wall.

ut_east_gate_buttress.blurb: The eastern section of Gate Buttress in Little Cottonwood Canyon, a wall of mostly trad lines with a smaller handful of sport routes. The grades center on 5.10 through 5.12, with a few easier and a lone harder line, so it suits climbers past the beginner Schoolroom stage. It is part of the same canyon-side buttress that holds some of the most popular crags in the Wasatch, and it catches sun on a southeast-facing exposure, which makes it pleasant in cool months and warm in summer.
ut_east_gate_buttress.parking_note: About 1.25 miles up Little Cottonwood Canyon, use the lot on the left or the roadside on the right.
ut_east_gate_buttress.approach: A trail leaves the lot toward the Gate Boulders; continue west and uphill through the regrown talus, staying on the established path to reach the crag.

ut_hurricave.blurb: A very steep limestone cave near the town of Hurricane, built for strong sport climbers. The routes are almost all in the 5.12 to 5.14 range, with the bulk at 5.13, on overhanging rock. The rock is somewhat chossy and the footing underfoot is loose, though belay stances were built flat and solid. Most lines have fixed draws, but not all. The cave faces west, so it fits cooler days: winter afternoons and spring or fall mornings are when it is comfortable, and the deepest lines hardly see sun.
ut_hurricave.parking_note: Follow Cliff Road out of Hurricane to a dirt road that ends at an established parking area.
ut_hurricave.approach: A steep trail with cairns climbs to the cave in about fifteen minutes.

ut_south_facing_wall_2.blurb: The larger of the two walls at the Hideaway, high on the north side of American Fork Canyon. It is a wide, steep limestone face with overhanging ground on the right, where blue mineral streaks are common. The moderates, mostly around 5.10, are on the left end, while the hard routes from 5.12 into the low 5.13s sit toward the right. All sport climbing. The wall faces southeast and stays shaded for a good part of the day in warm months, and sunny winter days can be pleasant. The hike in is long and steep for this canyon.

ut_black_table.blurb: A remote climbing area on the foothills of the Henry Mountains in south-central Utah, reached by dirt roads from Hanksville. Most of the climbing is trad on slabs, with a couple of boulder problems, and the grades sit mainly in the 5.10 to 5.12 range with a few easier lines. The rock is slick, thin and sometimes loose, with lichen in places, so expect serious, adventurous climbing where protection can be sparse. There is barely a trail, so plan for route-finding, and bring everything you need for a long day far from help.
ut_black_table.parking_note: From Hanksville, take Highway 95 east, turn onto road 276, then onto the BLM Black Table road, and park at the small pullout beside the fire ring below the foothill.
ut_black_table.approach: Cairns mark a line up the foothill into a meadow of boulders; the last stretch to the climbs has no trail.

ut_o_crags_three_finger_canyon.blurb: A cluster of sandstone crags in Three Finger Canyon, the busiest corner of the Eastern Reef, also called the Sandstone Alps, in the San Rafael Swell. It mixes long slab routes with shorter steeper lines in the side canyons. Most are trad, with some sport and a few aid climbs, and the grades cluster around 5.7 to 5.9, so it suits parties looking for moderate adventure. Pitches can be run out, so leaders should be comfortable above the stated grade. This is a remote, sun-exposed desert setting reached by a rough dirt road.
ut_o_crags_three_finger_canyon.parking_note: Leave the interstate, follow the dirt road to the entrance of Three Finger Canyon, then take the roughly two-mile rough track in; high clearance or four-wheel drive is wise.
